Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents

CCS: Security and privacy Software and application security
Yicheng Cai Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA email: yccai@psu.edu , Taegyu Kim Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA email: tgkim@psu.edu and Peng Liu Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA email: pxl20@psu.edu
© none
Abstract.

Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.

Keywords: 
Backtracking, Agent application, Intermediate abstraction, Indirect prompt injection, Memory poisoning

1. Introduction

Agent applications powered by large language models (LLMs) have been widely deployed. For example, an open-source agent application, GPT-Researcher, accumulated over 24,000 GitHub stars after release (GPT, 2025). Moreover, enterprise agent applications may increase from under 5% in 2025 to about 40% by the end of 2026, according to a recent Gartner forecast (Gartner, 2025).

Meanwhile, such agent applications are under threat from emerging agent-specific attacks, among which indirect prompt injection (IPI) (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b) and memory & context poisoning (MC-Poison) (Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025) are the most prevalent two of the OWASP Top 10 threats for agent applications (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025). For instance, a number of IPI CVEs (Cur, 2025; 5ir, 2025; Neu, 2025; Rehberger, wunderwuzzi) and MC-Poison-based red-teaming (Rehberger, wunderwuzzi; Lyons, 2025; Goodin, 2025) have been reported across multiple commercial agent applications.

When a security incident occurs in deployed agent applications, organizations backtrack the incident in order to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are: (1) trajectory logs, which record a sequence of agent observations and actions (Zhu et al., 2025) mapping to agent functionalities, such as planning, acting by invoking tools, and recalling information from memory (Liu et al., 2025); (2) source code of the compromised applications. It is worth noting that application-specific function call logs are often fairly limited: developers may not anticipate which calls are diagnostically relevant to emerging agent-specific attacks and consequently omit the corresponding log printing statements (Yuan et al., 2012a), or complete logging is disabled due to overhead thresholds and privacy considerations (Zhao et al., 2017; Yuan et al., 2012b).

Motivating example. Consider an MC-Poison security incident on GPT-Researcher, where an analyst received an incident report from a user/victim of the application (Section 3.1). There are three stakeholders: the analyst, the remedy administrator (usually the user), and the developers. The analyst aimed to backtrack the incident to identify the CEP, i.e., the function call that first introduced the malicious content to the application (Section 4.3). When the corresponding input arguments of the CEP function call are already logged, the analyst can (1) provide the remedy admin with a concrete, actionable remedy, e.g., the exact poisoned file to remove from a knowledge base that may contain hundreds of documents in various formats; when the corresponding function call log entry is missing, the analyst can (2) deliver to the developers the log printing statement placement around the CEP function call, enabling more efficient logging that makes the application diagnosable for future incidents.

Identifying the CEPs requires significant manual effort from the analyst. The analyst first triaged and examined the trajectory log and narrowed down the suspect cause to a particular agent functionality (i.e., knowledge-base retrieval). However, it remains difficult to identify the CEPs based only on the agent functionality since one agent functionality typically corresponds to many function calls, and no trajectory log records concrete function calls (Listing 1). Fundamentally speaking, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while function calls are at a lower layer (i.e., the app code execution layer). Static analysis on the source code of the application can complement trajectory-log-based agent-functionality-level diagnosis by pinpointing the CEPs through variable-level taint analysis. However, the analysis is hindered by a large set of CEP candidates: only a small subset is associated with the suspected initial compromise. After log-based pruning, there are still 1,518 candidates left in GPT-Researcher source code; to infer if a candidate belongs to the suspected initial compromise, the analyst spent hours on manual code inspection, detailed in Section 3.1. The main reason is that the code around the candidates carries little agent functionality semantics, and the analyst needs to gather enough evidence along the corresponding code paths before making a deduction.

None of the existing approaches can provide stakeholders with the two “can provide” benefits mentioned in the motivating example, since trajectory-log-based failure diagnosis (Zhu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b), detection-based failure attribution (Kim et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Chocron et al., 2026), and preventive information flow control (Debenedetti et al., 2025) do not provide the analyst with the CEPs but faulty agent execution state (Zhu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026), faulty agent (Zhang et al., 2025b) or agent-owner (Chocron et al., 2026), and LLM tool calls (not function calls at the source code level) (Kim et al., 2025; Debenedetti et al., 2025) instead.

Our approach can provide stakeholders with the two benefits because it backtracks the security incident. As mentioned in the motivating example, narrowing the CEPs during backtracking requires significant manual effort since the analyst needs to do code inspection to recover the agent functionality semantics from the program source code. Our insight is to introduce a new intermediate abstraction (Section 4.4) that enables the analyst to write a few queries at the agent-functionality-level, and the query processing outputs can exclude irrelevant CEP candidates directly. However, identifying which CEP candidates semantically correspond to specific agent functionalities is hard since program structures and implementations vary, making it difficult to generalize how to identify the mapping relationships. Fortunately, we observe that agent functionalities can be grouped into a small number of regions depending on the type of information source (Section 2) with which they interact. Each region is a set of program variables that implement agent functionalities of the same group. The variables that receive the return values of the CEP candidates are also included. Based on this insight, we build a tool named Origin that realizes this abstraction as a graph across two layers. Origin takes as input the source code of an agent application and a small set of developer-provided labels, and produces the cross-layer graph that can be queried by analysts using a query language during security incident investigations: (i) narrow down candidates at the region level/layer, (ii) identify the CEPs at the variable level.

Challenges. Our approach poses two challenges. First, define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between two semantic layers: the agent functionality layer vs. the application code execution layer. Since the implementation of the same agent functionality by different agent applications varies (e.g., the functions/variables naming, the used agent frameworks), we believe such an intermediate abstraction can provide an analyst with the same interface when backtracking security incidents of different applications. Second, constructing the cross-layer graph (defined in the intermediate abstraction) requires determining which region each variable belongs to. This is because a variable’s region is determined by which information source its data came from or flows into, but a variable’s name, type, or enclosing function does not carry these semantics.

Solutions. For the first challenge, we design the Cross-Layer Dependency Graph (CLDG) (Section 5) that connects region-inferred functions to the underlying variables in the taint graph through cross-plane edges. We also design the associated query language. As in BackTracker (King and Chen, 2003), the essence of backtracking is dependence analysis. Since the agent application CEPs are specific function calls, static taint analysis is suitable to identify the two types of dependencies a backtracking tool can rely on: variable-level data dependencies and function-level data dependencies. For the second challenge, we design region inference (Section 6.3) that mimics the analyst’s code inspection process by rules, which requires only a small set of developer-provided labels and automatically infers the regions for the variables.

Contributions. We make the following contributions.

  • •

    We design the CLDG plus the associated query language, a new intermediate abstraction that bridges the semantic gap between agent-functionality-level reasoning and program-variable-level application code execution.

  • •

    We design region inference, a technique that maps program variables into the relevant regions by rule-guided propagation of label information to the relevant functions along tainted program paths.

  • •

    We build and evaluate Origin on five real-world agent applications across eight attack incidents. Origin correctly identifies every CEP with a single candidate per incident, reducing the analyst’s inspection scope by 64–94% compared to the full taint graph and replacing exhaustive source code inspection with region-guided diagnosis.

To foster research on this topic, we will release the source code of Origin to GitHub.

2. Background

Agent Applications. An LLM-powered agent application interacts with diverse information sources for implementing various agent functionalities (e.g., perceiving the user instructions, planning, acting by invoking tools, and recalling information from memory) (Liu et al., 2025). Such applications produce trajectory logs to record the invocations of agent functionalities during a concrete execution (Zhu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025). Two types of information sources are: (1) external information sources outside the applications, including but not limited to user inputs, interactions with humans or agents, sensor readings, network-accessible content (e.g., web pages and emails), and LLM-generated content; (2) internal information sources within the applications such as knowledge bases and memory. The memory stores multi-round interactions between the user and the agent, persisted on disk in either original or summarized form, so that the agent can recall prior context across sessions (Liu et al., 2025).

Attacks on Agent Applications. Agent-specific attacks such as IPI (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b) and MC-Poison (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025; Chen et al., 2024; Zou et al., 2025) compromise the agent applications by injecting manipulated content into legitimate information sources of the applications. MC-Poison attacks usually involve two phases that occur in separate executions: a poisoning phase, in which malicious data is written to an internal information source, and an exploitation phase, in which the stored data is retrieved and causes harm. In some incidents, poisoning occurs outside the application (e.g., an attacker directly modifies a knowledge base document), and only the exploitation phase is observable.

Static Taint Analyzers. Existing taint-analysis frameworks such as Joern (Joe, 2025), Pysa (Pys, 2026), and CodeQL (Cod, 2025b) can already compute propagation paths over program variables and expressions. These capabilities can be repurposed for backtracking agent application security incidents. However, they expose only program code-level semantics and do not provide abstractions aligned with agent functionalities.

3. Motivation

3.1. Motivating Example

Security Incident. Consider GPT-Researcher, an agent application that conducts research for users and generates synthesized content (GPT, 2025). A security analyst receives an incident report from a user of the application. The report states that the application produced a research synthesis containing incorrect information for one particular research task, while other tasks were completed correctly. The report includes: a description of how the application is used, a PDF of the research synthesis, a trajectory log (Zhu et al., 2025) of the application (Listing 1), and the application’s source code. According to the user description, the application used both a knowledge base and web data for this failed task. The analyst listed three likely accident causes: the LLM was hallucinating, the scraped webpages were manipulated, or the knowledge base was poisoned, where the latter two are security-oriented.

Three Stakeholders. There are three stakeholders in the incident: the analyst, the remedy administrator (usually the user), and the developers. The remedy admin needs a concrete, actionable remedy for the damage, e.g., removing the exact poisoned file from the knowledge base with hundreds of documents; the developers need the log printing statement placement suggestion that makes the application more diagnosable for future incidents, e.g., log the parameter values of the function call corresponding to the initial compromise immediately before that call (Listing 2, Line 83). To provide the two stakeholders with the two benefits, the analyst aimed to identify the CEP, i.e., the function call that first introduced the malicious content to the application (Section 4.3).

Log Triage. To identify the CEP of the incident, the analyst first triaged the trajectory log (Listing 1), which records the user task, the application’s research plan, links to scraped webpages, and HTTP requests to an LLM provider. These coarse-grained traces were sufficient to rule out LLM hallucination and manipulated webpages, leaving knowledge-base poisoning as the remaining suspect cause. However, the log could not help identify which function call is responsible for the initial compromise (i.e., retrieving poisoned content from the knowledge base), because the trajectory log did not record concrete function calls. Fundamentally speaking, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while function calls are at the app code execution layer.

Static Taint Analysis. To identify the CEP, the analyst complemented the trajectory-log-based agent-functionality-level diagnosis by variable-level static taint analysis on the application’s source code. The analysis extracted 1,895 API calls as taint source candidates, i.e., function calls that could potentially introduce untrusted content. Using distinctive log patterns (e.g., “Starting research for …” colored red in Listing 1), the analyst located the corresponding log printing statements in the source code, identified their callers, and pruned program paths that cannot reach the callers, filtering out candidates on irrelevant paths. This log-guided pruning reduced the candidates from 1,895 to 1,518, but the analyst still needs to determine which of these candidates are related to knowledge-base retrieval functionality.

Manual Code Inspection Burden. Without tool support to filter candidates by their functionality, the analyst’s only option is to inspect each candidate manually. Yet even determining whether a candidate is related to knowledge-base retrieval requires multi-step code inspection. For instance, to determine that the candidate loader.load() in Listing 2 retrieves facts from a knowledge base, the analyst had to (a) trace the variable loader back to its definition, (b) examine each class in loader_dict and its load function, and (c) combine these observations with the caller name _load_document to infer the developer’s intent. Repeating this process across 1,518 candidates would take hours.

3.2. Limitations of Existing Approaches

Existing approaches for analyzing and defending agent applications cannot provide stakeholders with the two benefits illustrated above. The main reason is that trajectory-log-based failure diagnosis (Zhu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b), detection-based failure attribution (Kim et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026; Chocron et al., 2026), and preventive information flow control (Debenedetti et al., 2025) do not provide the analyst with the CEPs. They instead provide the analyst with the faulty agent execution state (Zhu et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) (e.g., an agent forming an incorrect plan), faulty agent (Zhang et al., 2025b) or agent-owner (Chocron et al., 2026), and LLM tool calls (not function calls at the source code level) (Kim et al., 2025; Debenedetti et al., 2025).

4. Approach Overview

4.1. Scope

Existing agent applications can be classified into two categories: predefined workflow (C1), where application source code rather than LLM decides control flow among agent functionalities; OpenClaw-like agents (Ope, 2026; Her, 2026; Aut, 2025) (C2), where the LLM decides at runtime which agent functionality to invoke next. The C2 agents have recently emerged; however, most existing applications belong to C1. Our approach is directly motivated by C1, not by C2. Hence, the scope of this work is C1; C2 and agent library frameworks (Lan, 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Smo, 2025) are out of scope and remain an area for future research.

4.2. Threat Model

We assume that adversaries can launch two categories of agent-specific attacks by methods proposed in existing works: IPI (Greshake et al., 2023) and MC-Poison (Dong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024). The two attack classes are the most prevalent among the OWASP Top 10 threats for agent applications and can cover all the risk categories in the report that target agent functionalities of the applications (OWASP GenAI Security Project, 2025). The remaining categories are either risks inherited from traditional software security (i.e., remote code execution, privilege escalation, and supply chain integrity), or those reside outside the application (i.e., inter-agent communication protocol, social engineering, and insider threats). Note: the non-protocol part of the insecure inter-agent communication risk category can be caused by IPI and MC-Poison. Such an attack incident is investigated in Section 9.3.

4.3. Compromise Entry Point

The agent-specific attack classes in Section 4.2 share a common characteristic: malicious data enters the application through the return value of an API call and propagates through data flow to cause harm. We define the compromise entry point (CEP) based on the characteristic and standard static taint tracking (Yin et al., 2007). Given a security incident in an agent application, the CEP is identified by: (i) the name of the API call whose return value contains the malicious data, (ii) the name of the corresponding source code program file, and (iii) the line number of the call site. We also provide the analyst with a set of taint propagation paths, where each path starts from a variable receiving the return value of the CEP function call and ends at a variable capturing the attack effect. Each variable in the paths is contained in exactly one function. Mapping each variable to its enclosing function gives a function-level path: the sequence of functions through which the data passes from entry to effect.

4.4. Problem Statement

Our insight: the need for an intermediate abstraction. As the motivating example illustrates, the analyst reasons about executed agent functionalities observed from the trajectory log (e.g., “which code retrieves from the knowledge base?”), while static taint analysis operates at the level of program variables. However, no existing static analysis technique can determine which program variables semantically correspond to which specific agent functionalities, because program structures and naming conventions vary across applications, making it hard to generalize such a mapping.

Fortunately, we observe that agent functionalities can be grouped into a small number of groups based on the type of information source (Section 2) with which they interact. For instance, retrieving from a knowledge base and recalling memory are distinct functionalities, but both interact with internal information sources; hence, they belong to the same group. We call such a group a region: a set of program variables that collectively implement agent functionalities of the same group. An analyst can query at the region level (e.g., “which region is for retrieving content from the knowledge base?”); the query processing outputs can exclude irrelevant CEP candidates directly, without manual code inspection.

Concretely, the intermediate abstraction is composed of four elements: (1) a region set that partitions agent functionalities into finite groups; (2) a region-to-variable mapping that associates each region with the program variables that implement it; (3) a region-level query interface (including the query language) through which analysts express their diagnostic queries in terms of regions rather than variables; (4) a region-to-variable query mapping that translates region-level queries into variable-level queries, supported by existing static analysis infrastructure. The goal of this work is to design a tool that realizes the new abstraction.

4.5. Challenges

Challenge 1: Define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between two semantic layers: agent functionality layer vs. the application code execution layer. The implementation of the same agent functionality by different agent applications varies (e.g., the functions/variables naming, the used agent frameworks). We believe such an intermediate abstraction is needed so that an analyst can use the same interface for backtracking security incidents of different applications.

Challenge 2: Constructing the region-to-variable mapping. The abstraction requires a concrete mapping from regions to program variables (element 2). No existing static analysis technique can infer agent functionalities from program source code. As illustrated in Section 3.1, variable names, such as ret_data, loader_dict, and loader in the function _load_document, do not carry the hints that they are used for retrieving from a knowledge base. Therefore, it is hard to determine which region they belong to.

4.6. Origin Overview

Origin takes as input (1) the source code of an agent application and (2) developer-provided labels. It outputs a CLDG that analysts query to identify the CEPs of security incidents on the agent application. Figure 1 illustrates Origin.

CLDG (Section 5). The CLDG is a two-plane directed graph: The function plane is a set of region-inferred function nodes (abstraction element 1 in Section 4.4); the cross-plane edges connect each function to the variables in the variable plane (element 2). The CLDG, together with the associated query language (elements 3 and 4, Section 7), addresses Challenge 1.

CLDG Construction (Section 6). Origin (i) performs forward taint propagation from the return values of every API call in the source code to build the variable plane of the CLDG (Section 6.2); (ii) uses the developer-provided labels (Section 6.1) as input for region inference (Section 6.3), which classifies each function to a region (addressing Challenge 2).

Query Processing (Section 7). The analyst first submits a region-level query against the CLDG; then inspects the returned graph to identify the source/sink variables for a variable-level query (Section 7). The output is the CEP and the corresponding paths in Section 4.3.

5. Cross-Layer Dependency Graph

The CLDG realizes the intermediate abstraction as a directed graph of two planes: the function plane and the variable plane.

Definition 5.0 (Cross-Layer Dependency Graph).

Let PP be an agent application with the function set ℱ\mathcal{F}. The Cross-Layer Dependency Graph G=(ℛ,Vfn,λ,Ecross,Vvar,Evar)G=(\mathcal{R},\,V_{\mathrm{fn}},\,\lambda,\,E_{\mathrm{cross}},\,V_{\mathrm{var}},\,E_{\mathrm{var}}) of PP is a two-plane directed graph, where:

  • •

    Region set. ℛ\mathcal{R} is a mapping from each region name to a set of agent functionalities. Each agent functionality is a mapping from the functionality name to a set of functions in the agent application program. Five representative regions (detailed in Appendix A) are: Per (Perceiving), PA (Planning & Acting), RR (Recalling & Reflecting), PK (Prompt Kitchen), and UNK (Unknown).

  • •

    Function plane. Vfn⊆ℱV_{\mathrm{fn}}\subseteq\mathcal{F} is the set of functions reachable from all API calls in PP via taint propagation. λ:Vfn→ℛ∪{UNK}\lambda\colon V_{\mathrm{fn}}\to\mathcal{R}\cup\{\mathrm{UNK}\} assigns each function node its inferred region.

  • •

    Variable plane. VvarV_{\mathrm{var}} is the set of program variables reachable from all API calls in PP via taint propagation, and Evar⊆Vvar×VvarE_{\mathrm{var}}\subseteq V_{\mathrm{var}}\times V_{\mathrm{var}} is the set of taint edges among them. The same variable in different code statements is treated as different nodes (with different identifiers) in the variable plane.

  • •

    Cross-plane edges. Ecross⊆Vfn×VvarE_{\mathrm{cross}}\subseteq V_{\mathrm{fn}}\times V_{\mathrm{var}} connects each function node ff to every program variable defined/used in ff.

The region set ℛ\mathcal{R} can be determined by the security analyst as long as the mapping relation is provided. Our design is applicable to any analyst-defined region set. Once a particular region set is adopted, Origin requires a corresponding function-to-information-source mapping table from developers of the agent application (Section 6.1). In addition, every cross-function taint edge in the variable plane is naturally mapped to an edge connecting two functions. Such edges appear on the function-level paths mentioned in Section 4.3.

6. CLDG Construction

Constructing the CLDG involves two steps: (1) taint propagation to build its variable plane (Section 6.2) and (2) infer regions for nodes in the planes (Section 6.3). Step (2) requires developer knowledge as input (Section 6.1).

6.1. Developer Knowledge Collection

Origin runs with a function-to-information-source mapping table showing which functions in an application interact with external (EXT) or internal (INT) information sources. This information is collected once from the agent application developer and reused across all incident investigations.

Well-trained developers know only functions that directly call built-in or library APIs need examination, but they may still find it time-consuming to label this subset of functions, e.g., 353 out of 607 functions in GPT-Researcher. As in Listing 3, to determine whether an API call execute() accesses an internal information source (INT), the developer needs to (1) trace variable commons back to common_dependencies function definition to identify the Supabase client, (2) check the preceding calls before execute() against the API documentation to determine that execute() retrieves content from the chat_history table, and (3) confirm that the chat_
history table is used as agent memory. The developer needs to examine all remaining API calls in the function to ensure they are not interacting with external (EXT) information sources (e.g., a user, an LLM, or a web browser) before assigning a label INT to the function.

To address this, we use an LLM with a prompt containing the function’s API calls, relevant source code, and rules for identifying information sources. The LLM produces a structured report: a decision for each call, its explanation, supporting code locations, and any missing information for labeling a function (Appendix F.1). Although human validation is still needed, this reduces the developer’s work from labeling to reviewing a report. The experiment results show that the knowledge collection speed increases by 15.4–75.0% and the accuracy increases by 8.3–50.4% (Section 10.8).

6.2. Taint Graph Construction

With the developer labels in place, Origin constructs the graph. The variable plane (VvarV_{\mathrm{var}}, EvarE_{\mathrm{var}}) is produced by performing context-, flow-, field-sensitive forward taint propagation from the return values of every API call (implementation described in Section 8). Because propagation starts from all API calls, any CEP function call that matches the definition in Section 4.3 lies on a path in the variable plane and is locatable by queries against the CLDG. VfnV_{\mathrm{fn}} and EcrossE_{\mathrm{cross}} are derived from the variable plane: f∈Vfnf\in V_{\mathrm{fn}} if any of its variables appears in VvarV_{\mathrm{var}}; EcrossE_{\mathrm{cross}} connects each function to its variables.

6.3. Region Inference

The region inference algorithm implements the region-to-variable mapping element in the abstraction (Section 4.4). The goal is to classify the functions in the function plane of CLDG into the five regions detailed in Appendix A.

We observe that a naive feature-based clustering approach, i.e., clustering by function names, API names, or program code syntactic features, is not suitable for this task: (1) functions/APIs of the same name could implement completely different agent functionality in different agent applications, and thus belong to different regions. For example, two functions named load may read a webpage (fall into the PA region) or read a file from a knowledge base (fall into the RR region). Similarly, (2) syntactically similar string operations, e.g., x.format(y), may be used for prompt assembly or for non-agent functionalities, e.g., composing an error message.

Fortunately, we find that an analyst, fully aware of the semantics of the five regions, usually gathers evidence during code inspection to answer four questions, and the fusion of the answers can determine which region a function belongs to: (1) does the function interact with information source(s)? (2) does the function read from or write to the information source(s), or do both? (3) if the function interacts with multiple information source(s), which type of information source dominates (Section 2)? and (4) is the function mainly assembling prompts to appear in the LLM context window? Origin uses two categories of rules to mimic the aforementioned analyst’s reasoning process during code inspection for region inference:

Label propagation rules (3 in total) mimic the process of gathering evidence to answer the four questions about a function. Two rules propagate (along the tainted paths) the labels of the API calls that interact with information sources. Concretely, the two rules are: (1) if an API call reads an information source, propagate the label forward; (2) if an API call writes an information source, propagate the label backward. We also have a rule for propagating a special label of function calls that assemble prompts rather than interact with information sources. Prompt-assembly-related function calls are assigned with such a label (e.g., text-composition functions like format; function names or parameters with special names consisting of “prompt”). This rule propagates labels only within a function because we observe that prompt assembly is an agent functionality local to discrete function(s).

Condition-action rules (9 in total, Table 1) mimic the analyst’s reasoning process of region determination by combining answers to the four questions against the gathered evidence. For example, if a function receives a user request, it gathers the label of an external information source and no label of prompt assembly according to the label propagation rules; consequently, it is classified into the Per region, which only passively reads external information sources.

Our evaluation shows that the two categories of rules work well in practice (Section 10.4). Meanwhile, our condition-action rules are intended to be practical rather than exhaustive. Initially, we observed that agents usually prepare a prompt shortly before writing to the LLM context window. Therefore, we only have Rule 8 for the PK region, since LLMs are treated as external information sources in Origin. However, our case studies later showed that prompt assembly can also begin shortly after reading any information source, without immediately passing the partial prompt to the LLM context window. We added Rule 9 to cover this case.

7. Query Processing

Given a constructed CLDG, the analyst investigates a security incident by issuing queries against it using a query language.

7.1. Query Language

The query language implements the region-level query interface element in the abstraction (Section 4.4). The full grammar is provided in Appendix B.

Each query begins with the keyword CHECK, followed by one or more atomic formulas joined by logical connectives. An atomic formula consists of the predicate DEPENDS_ON, which asserts a taint data flow between two terms. A term can be either a region name or a program variable identifier, allowing queries at the region level or the variable level. Logical connectives include AND and OR. For example, CHECK (PK DEPENDS_ON PA) AND (PA DEPENDS_ON PK) is a commonly used region-level query for backtracking IPI incidents by an analyst (Table 5). The atom PK DEPENDS_ON PA asks whether data from the PA region (e.g., the crawled webpage), can flow into the PK region (e.g., to assemble a prompt). Similarly, the atom PA DEPENDS_ON PK asks whether data in the PK region (e.g., the assembled prompt) can flow back to the PA region (e.g., the LLM takes the prompt as input and the generated content flows to write a document).

The language also provides a chaining operator →\rightarrow: the formula after →\rightarrow is evaluated against the subgraph returned by the preceding formula, allowing the analyst to progressively narrow down the variable-level results. For example, after writing the aforementioned region-level query, an analyst can write →\rightarrow, followed by a second region/variable-level query. Origin first evaluates the first query; if the result is not empty, it continues to evaluate the second query against the result of the first query (Section 7.2).

7.2. Query Evaluation

This subsection implements the region-to-variable query mapping element of abstraction (Section 4.4).

Region-Level Query Evaluation. A region-level query, such as CHECK PA DEPENDS_ON RR, returns a data dependency graph over function nodes through two steps: (1) identify the variables in RsrcR_{\mathrm{src}} functions and the variables in RsinkR_{\mathrm{sink}} functions by using λ\lambda and EcrossE_{\mathrm{cross}}; (2) compute forward reachability from the RsrcR_{\mathrm{src}} variables and backward reachability from the RsinkR_{\mathrm{sink}} variables in the variable plane, producing two sets of reachable variable nodes. The intersection of these two sets contains all variables that lie on some taint path from RsrcR_{\mathrm{src}} to RsinkR_{\mathrm{sink}}. An edge (f1,f2)(f_{1},f_{2}) appears in the result if a taint edge in EvarE_{\mathrm{var}} connects a variable in f1f_{1} to a variable in f2f_{2} within this intersection. When a query contains logical connectives, AND and OR combine result graphs by intersection and union of their node and edge sets, respectively.

Variable-Level Query Evaluation. In a variable-level query, the source and sink are specified by their node identifiers in the variable plane (visible when the analyst inspects a function’s variables in the region-level query result). For example, CHECK node.5110 DEPENDS_ON node.4216 queries whether there is a taint path from variable 4216 to variable 5110. To evaluate the variable-level query, a naive graph slicing of the CLDG variable plane may include paths that are not feasible in any real execution. Origin uses the application’s call graph and control flow graphs constructed during CLDG construction to enumerate only the control-flow feasible taint paths between the source and sink variables. The returned paths are variable-level taint paths. As mentioned in Section 4.3, the taint paths can be naturally mapped to the corresponding function-level paths.

8. Implementation

We implement Origin as a Python program (∼\sim16 KLoC) on top of Joern (v4.0.360) (Cod, 2025a), with type inference enhancement by Pyrefly (v0.45.0) (Fac, 2026). We address three limitations of Joern that cause false negatives in taint propagation. First, Joern does not parse generator expressions; we rewrite yield and yield from to return before analysis. Second, taint stored in class instance variables (e.g., self.x) is not tracked across functions; we propagate it explicitly via control-flow graph reachability. Third, Joern’s call graph is incomplete under dynamic dispatch. We first incorporate type-informed indirect call resolution by patching Pyrefly (Fac, 2026); then we infer the targets of indirect calls by following Xia et al. (Xia et al., 2024) and Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2024a) with two enhancements: context-sensitive type chain tracking in place of a global type-chain map, and value set analysis in place of full data-flow analysis.

9. Case Studies

We now discuss our experience applying Origin to backtracking security incidents on real-world agent applications.

Selected Applications. We have chosen five actively maintained open-source agent applications (Table 2): two single-agent applications (SAAs) and three multi-agent applications (MAAs) with substantial real-world adoption, from four major domains, i.e., deep research (DR), conversational assistant (CA), coding copilot (CC), and software development (SD).

Investigated Security Incidents. Our eight investigated incidents are diverse in attack entry points and attack classes. As shown in Table 3, we cover both IPI (Greshake et al., 2023) and MC-Poison (Dong et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2024) attack classes, where MC-Poison is further divided into the subclasses of memory poisoning (M) and knowledge-base poisoning (KB); one incident is on a compound attack that combines IPI and MC-Poison (KB). Beyond directly modifying files on the file system (e.g., the GPT-Researcher MC-Poison (KB) incident in the motivating example), we also consider attack scenarios where the malicious data enters through the application’s user interface: for instance, in the Quivr MC-Poison (M) incident, the attacker sent a crafted chat message that poisoned the memory of the agent.

9.1. Shared Backtracking Workflows

The analyst’s backtracking workflows are similar across the investigated incidents, despite the diversity in attack classes and entry points. Specifically, the analyst (i) identifies the suspect agent functionality from the trajectory log, (ii) submits a region-level query, (iii) inspects the resulting graph to identify variable-level taint source/sink candidates, (iv) selects the source/sink to submit a variable-level query, and (v) identifies the CEP and the corresponding paths. Typically, a CEP identification requires two queries (Table 3): one region-level query to narrow down the scope and one variable-level query to pinpoint the CEP. We show in Section 9.2 that inspecting the resulting graph of a region-level query usually narrows down the source/sink candidates for a variable-level query to one or two, respectively. With the knowledge obtained from the trajectory logs, the analyst can have a suspect ranking for source and sink candidates (detailed in Appendix C). In our case studies, these help the analyst submit the correct variable-level query with minimal trials. Besides, for attack incidents that span multiple phases in separate executions (e.g., Quivr MC-Poison (M)), the analyst repeats steps (i)–(iv) for each phase before identifying the CEP.

We observe that the variable-level query result, presented as a set of function-level paths, is typically sufficient for the analyst to identify and understand the CEP without inspecting the underlying variable-level taint propagation paths. In the Quivr MC-Poison (M) incident, the attack spans two phases (Section 2). The analyst submitted one variable-level query for each phase and obtained two valid function-level paths. Although the two paths correspond to two executions within different time periods, the analyst identified the shared function call arguments (i.e., the chat_history table of Supabase) in the source node (blue, RR region) of Phase A path and sink node (blue) of Phase B path. This indicated that the malicious content can be first written to the agent memory in a chat with the attacker; then be retrieved back in another chat with the user. Therefore, the CEP is identified as the function call to the user-chat interface. The full incident and its backtracking process are detailed in Appendix C.1. For simpler single-phase incidents such as the motivating GPT-Researcher MC-Poison (KB) case, the analyst can directly identify the CEP by examining the function-level paths returned by a variable-level query (detailed in Appendix C.2).

9.2. Common Practices for Graph Inspection

We report the common practices in step (iii) graph inspection, which replaces the time-consuming source code inspection:

(a) Not all nodes in the resulting graph of a region-level query require inspection. The graph contains nodes from the regions specified in the query as well as nodes from other regions that appear because they lie on the taint paths between the queried regions. Each node is colored by its region, so the analyst usually focuses only on nodes whose colors correspond to the queried regions and skips the rest. For example, in the Quivr MC-Poison (M) incident (phase A), the region-level query returns a graph of 21 function nodes, but only the 3 Per nodes (green) and 5 RR nodes (blue) match the queried regions and need examination (Figure 2(a)).

(b) Among the relevant nodes, it requires examining only a small number (usually less than 10) of function names and an even smaller number (usually 2 or 3) of variable-plane taint subgraphs corresponding to the functions. As in Figure 2(a), to identify the taint sink, the analyst examined the names of 3 green nodes of Per region, found create_question_handler relevant to the incident, and clicked it to reveal a variable-plane taint subgraph of a single node (Figure 3 in Appendix) that is identified as the sink candidate. The analyst then takes a similar process to identify the taint source candidate from the 5 blue nodes of RR region. The entire process requires only examining 8 function names and 2 taint subgraphs, which is a huge manual effort reduction compared to 2,615 LoC of Quivr’s source code inspection (Table 2). Origin also provides features that help the analyst handle larger graphs more efficiently, which are detailed in Appendix C.2 (Figure 4) and Appendix C.4 (Figure 5).

9.3. Notable Findings on Individual Applications

We report other notable observations from the case studies.

(a) An agentic loop within an execution does not prevent Origin from identifying the CEP, as long as both the CEP and the function call corresponding to the attack effect lie outside the loop. In the SWE-agent IPI incident, for example, each iteration of the agent loop in the attack execution queries the LLM for the next tool to invoke, executes that tool, and feeds the result back. However, since the loop appears in the middle of the returned taint path as pass-through functions and static taint analysis tracks data flow through variables in the source code, the taint propagation from source to sink remains intact, and Origin correctly identifies the CEP.

(b) When the source and sink functions are generic utilities shared by two or more agent functionalities in the application, specifying an intermediate variable as a waypoint is helpful in constraining the returned paths to the incident-relevant subset. In both aider and MetaGPT, a single pair of file read/write functions (read_text/write_text in aider; aread/awrite in MetaGPT) serves as the major file I/O interface across the entire codebase. A standard source-to-sink query between these functions returns a large set of taint paths between file-read and file-write in the application, the majority of which are unrelated to the incident. We observe a good practice for getting a more incident-related result, i.e., identifying an intermediate function from the region-level query result and specifying a variable within it as a waypoint. These functions are identifiable because trajectory logs record semantically meaningful steps (e.g., named commands and task-level actions) that map directly to function-plane nodes in the CLDG.

(c) Origin can handle an attack incident rooted in inter-agent communication manipulation. In MetaGPT, the identified CEP (aread) reads a specification file that the upstream architect agent planned and wrote to disk (the file is compromised by an attacker); the downstream engineer agent reads malicious data and generates code according to a manipulated task. The coordination mechanism between agents (i.e., shared files on disk) functions exactly as designed. However, due to a lack of verification for the artifacts produced by a previous execution, the IPI happened across agent boundaries through the application’s normal coordination mechanism.

10. Evaluation

10.1. Research Questions (RQs)

We evaluate Origin on the same set of security incidents as in Section 9 to answer the following research questions: (RQ1) Can analysts use Origin to correctly identify the CEPs and the corresponding paths of the eight security incidents? (RQ2) How accurately does the region inference algorithm assign functions to regions? (RQ3) To what extent does Origin reduce the portion of the CLDG that analysts must inspect compared to using static taint analysis alone? (RQ4) What are the execution time and memory costs of Origin? (RQ5) How much developer knowledge is needed for region inference? (RQ6) How useful is the LLM-generated report?

10.2. Experimental Setup

All experiments are conducted on a machine with an Intel Core Ultra 9 285 CPU, 128 GB RAM, running Ubuntu 24.04. We use the human-validated function-to-information-source mapping table (Section 6.1) for all RQ evaluations.

10.3. CEP + Path Identification Correctness (RQ1)

Success Criteria. A diagnosis is considered successful iff the ground truth CEP and corresponding taint propagation path (the one matching the actual attack execution) defined in Section 4.3 are identified.

Results. As shown in Table 3, an analyst using Origin correctly identified the CEPs of all eight incidents, each having a single CEP candidate. The analyst can identify the CEPs by submitting two queries in five incidents and four queries in the other three incidents.

Comparison with Existing Tools. We also evaluate existing static taint analyzers, i.e., Joern (Joe, 2025), CodeQL (Cod, 2025b) and Pysa (Pys, 2026), on the same incidents. Since they lack the intermediate abstraction compared to Origin, we assume the tools are provided with the ground-truth source (i.e., the CEP) and sink as input and evaluate if analysts can use the tools to verify the correctness of the CEP. Specifically, for Joern and CodeQL: Success means the correct taint propagation path is identified and Fail means the opposite; For Pysa: Success means at least one reported function call lies on the correct taint propagation path; Fail means the expected function on the correct path is not reported.

As shown in Table 4, the tools fail on most incidents, primarily due to unresolved indirect call targets, missing data dependencies through language constructs, API calls, and first-writes-later-reads of object attributes, files, or databases (Appendix E). For example, in SWE-agent IPI, Joern fails to propagate taint through nested dictionary accesses. In Quivr MC-Poison (M), CodeQL fails to propagate taint from an LLM API call argument to its returned value because it does not model the corresponding library. In GPT-Researcher MC-Poison (KB), Pysa fails to resolve the target of an application function call, interrupting taint propagation from a variable used within the callee to a returned variable in the caller.

The limited data-flow information in Pysa’s output is insufficient for the analyst to identify the CEPs. For example, in MetaGPT IPI incident, Pysa reports four function calls, of which only one (WriteCode.run at write_code.py:142) lies on the correct path. When comparing against the path of 14 functions returned by Origin, WriteCode.run is the 4th function on the path: 3 functions from the CEP aread and 10 functions from the attack effect awrite. Therefore, the analyst would need extra analysis to identify the CEP.

10.4. Region Inference Accuracy (RQ2)

Table 6 reports region inference accuracy per application. For each function in VfnV_{\mathrm{fn}}, the algorithm classifies it into one of the four regions (excluding UNK). The description of the region set and the ground truth region distribution across the applications can be found in Appendix A.

Across all five applications, precision and recall range from 0.70 to 0.88. aider exhibits the lowest accuracy because the coding copilot provides a set of commands to use interactively (e.g., adding files, prompting the LLM, committing edits) rather than the application chaining them automatically. Origin produces short, disjoint taint paths for each aider command, and labels propagated from an API call along one taint path (detailed in Section 6.3) cannot reach functions that belong to a different command’s taint path.

10.5. Inspection Scope Reduced by Region-level Queries (RQ3)

Region-level queries can significantly reduce the graph inspection scope for the analyst. We measure this by comparing |Vq||V_{q}|, the number of variable-plane nodes in the region-level query result, against |Vvar||V_{\mathrm{var}}|, the full variable plane of the CLDG. Lower |Vq|/|Vvar||V_{q}|/|V_{\mathrm{var}}| means the analyst encounters a smaller fraction of the taint graph. As shown in Table 5, across all incidents, region-level queries reduce the variable plane to between 6.49% and 35.76% of its original size. We note that:

(a) PK is a key factor in this reduction and appears in 9 of the 11 region-level queries. This is because PK is where data from other regions converges to be assembled into the LLM prompt, and it typically contains very few functions (e.g., 1 in Quivr, 2 in aider, 3 in SWE-agent; more details in Appendix A). When a query involves PK, the returned graph is limited to function nodes that are transitively connected to this small set of PK functions, which substantially reduces the number of variable-plane nodes the analyst must inspect.

(b) The reduction ratio also depends on the size of the regions involved in the query, which varies across applications. The IPI incidents across the four applications use the same query CHECK (PK DEPENDS_ON PA) AND (PA DEPENDS_ON PK), yet the ratios range from 9.56% (SWE-agent) to 35.76% (GPT-Researcher). Regarding the ratio difference, we observe that a larger PA in an application often gives a larger result graph: PA contains 133 of 244 functions in GPT-Researcher but only 64 of 160 in SWE-agent (more details in Appendix A).

10.6. Performance of Origin (RQ4)

Table 7 reports the execution time and peak memory usage (Mem.) for each incident. Three stages of Origin execution time are reported separately: CLDG construction (CLDG), region inference (Infer.), and the queries evaluation time of each application averaged on corresponding incidents (Q¯\bar{Q}).

CLDG construction dominates execution time, accounting for over 95% of the total in every application. CLDG construction and region inference are one-time offline costs. The set of query evaluations is the only per-incident cost, and they were completed in under 90 ms across all five applications on average. Peak memory remains under 7 GB.

10.7. Required Developer Knowledge Amount (RQ5)

Table 8 reports the number of application functions and the numbers of EXT/INT labels, with the total number of labels also expressed as a percentage of application functions. Across the five applications, only 2.4%–8.9% of functions receive labels, indicating that Origin requires only a small amount of application-specific knowledge from developers.

10.8. Utility of LLM-Generated Report (RQ6)

Human Study Setup. We recruit four participants with different levels of agent-application knowledge and Python familiarity to examine whether the EXT/INT report benefits users with different backgrounds. Each participant completes two 10-minute tests: manual labeling (M) and LLM report’s label validation (L). In the M test, participants follow the developer workflow described in Section 6.1. In the L test, participants are provided with the LLM-generated report. We prepare two non-overlapping sets, A and B, each containing 200 functions from the five applications, so that participants do not encounter the same function twice. We set up a one-to-one mapping between the four participants and the four test sequences: MA→LBM_{A}\!\to\!L_{B}, LA→MBL_{A}\!\to\!M_{B}, MB→LAM_{B}\!\to\!L_{A}, and LB→MAL_{B}\!\to\!M_{A}, where subscripts identify the function sets. This counterbalancing reduces the influence of the test order and differences between the function sets.

Before the tests, we provide a labeling guide and 15 functions for practice, followed by 15 functions to check their understanding. We also provide an example showing participants how to use the report’s explanations and code references to validate its proposed labels. We measure speed as the number of functions labeled during the given 10 minutes and accuracy in terms of the reference answers, including decisions that neither label is needed.

Results. Table 9 reports speed changes relative to M (Δ\DeltaSpeed), accuracy in L (Acc.L\mathrm{Acc.}_{L}), and accuracy differences between L and M in percentage points (Δ\DeltaAcc.). All four participants achieve higher labeling speed and accuracy in the L test. Speed increases by 15.4–75.0%, while accuracy improves by 8.3–50.4 percentage points, reaching 88.9–100%.

11. Discussion

Framework-Induced Indirect Call Resolution. Our static analysis cannot resolve framework-induced indirect call targets (e.g., LangChain (Lan, 2025) tool dispatch). This causes the corresponding taint propagation path to be missing from the CLDG. Addressing this limitation requires either framework-specific modeling or dynamic analysis, which is future work.

Agents with An LLM-driven Agentic Loop. Autonomous agents such as OpenClaw (Ope, 2026) and Hermes (Her, 2026) are driven by an agentic loop in which, for each iteration, the LLM decides at runtime which agent functionality to invoke next. For such agents, static analysis alone cannot determine the CEP function call (e.g., which tool introduced the malicious data), except for the case discussed in Section 9.3, Finding (b). This remains an area for future research.

12. Related Work

Root Cause Analysis for Software Systems. Diagnosing the root cause of exploits and failures in software systems is the first step to repairing programs. Most existing works are based on backtracking (Xu et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2025), reconstruction (Cui et al., 2018; Ge et al., 2020; Yagemann et al., 2021; He et al., 2022), or statistical analysis (Blazytko et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024; Kasikci et al., 2015; Kasikci et al., 2017). These approaches focus on diagnosing the buggy code location(s) triggering memory safety violations (Xu et al., 2017; Cui et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2016; Chang et al., 2025; Cui et al., 2018; Yagemann et al., 2021; He et al., 2022; Blazytko et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024) and data races (Kasikci et al., 2015; Kasikci et al., 2017). However, in agent application security incidents, the application code itself is not buggy in terms of condition expressions and statement orders. The problem is that the application lacks validation or sanitization at the boundary between untrusted external information sources and the application. Consequently, the attacker-controlled data is entered through a legitimate API call and propagated through the pipeline unimpeded.

Causality Analysis for APT Attacks. A large body of work investigates APT attacks by constructing attack provenance graphs from OS-level audit logs (King and Chen, 2003; Milajerdi et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2018; Goyal et al., 2024). Subsequent work refines the granularity of logs by partitioning long-running processes into finer execution units (Ma et al., 2016; Ma et al., 2017; Ji et al., 2017) or by fusing application-layer logs with system audit data to recover application semantics (Hassan et al., 2020). The logs and audit data used in these systems are sufficient for analyzing traditional APT attacks. In agent applications, however, analysts rely on trajectory logs and static analysis on program code. Trajectory logs record agent behaviors at the agent functionality abstraction layer but miss the app-specific function call logging needed for pinpointing the CEP function calls. Static analysis does not provide the agent-functionality semantics that analysts need for reasoning. The bridging between the agent functionalities and the program code is difficult due to a semantic gap. Our work addresses this by implementing an intermediate abstraction that connects them.

Agent Application Attacks and Defenses. Agent attacks have targeted a wide range of commercial and open-source agents (Rehberger, 2024), most notably IPI attacks (Greshake et al., 2023; Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024b) and MC-Poison attacks (Chen et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024). In real-world settings, adversaries often employ compound attacks that combine both methods across different stages of agent execution (Zhang et al., 2025a).

Defenses have been proposed at multiple layers: data-instruction separation-based LLM hardening (Chen et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025b; Wallace et al., 2024) and prompt hardening (Hines et al., 2024) against IPI attacks, memory writes/retrieval-stage filtering against MC-Poison attacks (Xiang et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025; Sunil et al., 2026), and application-level taint tracking and policy enforcement at runtime (Debenedetti et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025; Costa et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025; Ji et al., 2026). All these defenses, however, are preventive in nature and can still be bypassed. When an attack does succeed, we still need to backtrack the initial compromise of the incident. In addition, detection of IPI attacks and MC-Poison attacks has been investigated in (Kim et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026) and (Tan et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025), respectively. However, detection and diagnosis (through backtracking) are two different problems.

13. Conclusion

We present Origin, a backtracking tool for security incidents in agent applications. Origin implements a new intermediate abstraction as CLDG, which connects region-inferred functions with variable-level taint subgraphs, and provides the associated query language that allows analysts to identify the CEPs with a small number of queries. Origin constructs the region-to-variable mapping in the CLDG by rule-guided region inference, which only takes a small set of developer-provided labels. Case studies on five applications and eight diverse attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin can correctly identify the CEPs of all incidents.
