Appendix A Configured Region Set

Region set. Our observations, consistent with prior work (Zhu et al., 2025), show that program variables serving the same agent functionality cluster naturally into five regions as follows:

  • •

    Perceiving (Per): Variables that receive input from external sources where the application does not initiate the interaction (e.g., user queries, incoming agent messages, sensor readings).

  • •

    Planning & Acting (PA): Variables that store LLM-generated responses and variables involved in application-initiated interactions with external sources (e.g., tool invocations, outgoing messages to other agents).

  • •

    Recalling & Reflecting (RR): Variables that retrieve information from internal sources (e.g., knowledge bases, experience repositories, execution logs) or store summarized experiences derived from prior activity.

  • •

    Prompt Kitchen (PK): Variables that assemble prompts for the LLM context window, which combine information drawn from the other three regions into a coherent input.

  • •

    Unknown (UNK): Variables that implement functionalities not belonging to the Per, PA, RR, or PK regions.

Region distribution across the evaluated applications with the configured region set. Table 10 reports the ground-truth classification of functions in each evaluated application using this region set. Here, |Vfn||V_{\mathrm{fn}}| is the total number of functions in the CLDG function plane; S denotes functions belonging to a single region, and M denotes functions spanning two or more regions.

Across all five applications, the multi-region ratio M:S stays at or below 6%, confirming that the vast majority of functions implement a single agent functionality and can be reliably classified to exactly one region. The few multi-region functions are those that orchestrate several agent functionalities within a single function; for example, ResearchConductor.conduct_research in GPT-Researcher retrieves context from web pages (PA), loads documents from the knowledge base (RR), and assembles prompts for the LLM (PK), thereby spanning three regions. The remaining functions in VfnV_{\mathrm{fn}} that do not belong to any region are utility functions that parse configuration files, log the execution trace, calculate token consumption, or handle errors; they are taint-reachable from CEP candidates and therefore included in VfnV_{\mathrm{fn}}, but they do not implement any agent functionality.

Appendix B Query Language Grammar

Appendix C Case Studies In-depth Details

We present details of four representative case studies that demonstrate the analyst’s backtracking workflow on different types of incidents.

C.1. Case Study 1: Quivr MC-Poison (M)

Incident. An attacker sends a crafted chat message through Quivr’s user interface. The message poisoned the memory database of Quivr. In a later chat session with the user, the malicious content is retrieved during question answering and reaches the LLM, producing a manipulated response.

Log investigation. The analyst triaged the trajectory log and found text of misinformation repeatedly appeared when the user asked questions about "Nvidia stock price". The log further showed that the files uploaded to the knowledge base did not contain the misinformation. The analyst deduced that Quivr’s memory database was poisoned.

CEP + path identification: exploitation phase. The analyst started to use Origin to identify the CEP. From the log, the analyst came up with the query on whether the malicious content in the memory database can pollute responses to the user. Consequently, the analyst submitted: CHECK (PK DEPENDS_ON RR) AND (Per DEPENDS_ON PK). The query returns a subgraph of the CLDG where each node is a function with attributes: node id, function name, and location (i.e., corresponding Python program file and line number of the function definition in the file). As shown in Figure 2(a), the graph contains 21 nodes, of which 3 are in the Per region (colored in green), 1 in the PK (red), and 5 in the RR (blue). Because the region-level query was submitted by the analyst, the analyst knew only the 3 nodes in the Per and 5 nodes in the RR need to be examined.

To formulate a variable-level query, the analyst needed to identify one or more variable-level taint sources in the RR and one or more variable-level taint sinks in the Per. The analyst began with the 3 nodes colored in green to identify the taint sinks. By examining the function names, the analyst identified two functions that may contain the taint sink candidates: create_question_handler and create_stream_
question_handler. From the log, the analyst found that the error traceback for the failed chat task passes through create_question_handler at chat_routes.py:197, confirming that this handler processed the incident request. The analyst clicked this node to reveal its variable plane. As shown in Figure 3, only one variable node appears: it holds the response to be delivered to the user. The analyst identified this variable (id 30064775110) as the taint sink.

The analyst then inspected the 5 RR nodes colored in blue. By examining function names, get_chat_history is the most relevant to retrieving content from the memory database. The analyst clicked it and found one variable that receives the return value of the Supabase retrieval API call. The analyst identified this variable (id 30064774216) as the taint source.

With the taint sink and taint source identified, the analyst submitted a variable-level query: CHECK node.30064775110 DEPENDS_ON node.30064774216. The query returns a set of paths in the variable plane that are mapped to 1 function-level path passing through 6 functions (Figure 2(b), phase A (left)). The path traces data from get_chat_history (RR) through _call_chain (PA, containing the API call to the LLM) to create_question_handler (Per), confirming that the poisoned content from the memory database went to the context window of the LLM and polluted the response that was delivered to the user.

CEP + path identification: poisoning phase. The taint source found in the exploitation phase might not be the CEP, because poisoning a memory database directly (Chen et al., 2024) is hard. Such an attack requires the attacker to (1) get the access credential to the user system; (2) to obtain the secret of the memory database running on the system; (3) to find the exact table in the memory database corresponding to the chat history of the user; (4) to identify the exact embedding model that the user is using and transform the malicious content into vectors using the model before inserting them into the table. Therefore, the analyst knew that the attacker is more likely to poison the memory database through user interfaces. With this, the analyst submitted: CHECK (PK DEPENDS_ON Per) AND (RR DEPENDS_ON PK).

The resulting subgraph contains 23 nodes. Similarly, the analyst only needed to examine 3 nodes in the Per (green) and 8 nodes in the RR (blue). The analyst went through a similar process of (1) examining the function names; (2) clicking interesting nodes to inspect their variable planes; (3) identifying the candidates for taint source and taint sink. As a result, the analyst identified one taint source and one taint sink and submitted a variable-level query: CHECK node.30064774368 DEPENDS_ON node.30064775110.

The query returns a set of paths in the variable plane that are mapped to 2 function-level paths. The path that corresponds to the execution in the incident is within them. As shown in Figure 2(b) (phase B (right)), it passes through 8 functions. The path traces data from create_question_hand
ler (Per) through _construct_prompt (PK), and _get_model
_response that sends the prompt to the LLM before saving the response into the chat history via update_chat_history.

CEP identified. The diagnosis results showed that the CEP of the attack incident is the API call in the create_
question_handler function that receives the HTTP request containing the malicious content at line number 152 in the file backend/routes/chat_routes.py.

C.2. Case Study 2: GPT-Researcher MC-Poison (KB)

This case study demonstrates how to backtrack the incident described in Section 3.1.

Region-level query. Following the workflow in Section C.1, the analyst submitted a region-level query CHECK (PK DEPEN
DS_ON RR) AND (PA DEPENDS_ON PK), which returns 135 functions (8 in RR, 41 in PK, 64 in PA).

Variable-level taint sink candidate identification. The analyst started with 64 PA nodes colored in yellow. Since the attack effect is a PDF file of manipulated research synthesis that was downloaded by the user, the analyst proactively searched for functions that write content to file when examining the function names of nodes. The analyst quickly found that only functions whose names start with write are relevant to the functionality. To get a cleaner view of the graph, the analyst utilized the features of Origin to filter out irrelevant nodes and edges: (1) using regular expression .*write.* to batch select the relevant nodes; (2) choosing the option to preserve only call-out edges in the graph. The filtered subgraph is shown in Figure 4, which contains only 10 nodes with edges showing who calls who in the call chain. The analyst could easily deduce that write_md_to_pdf is more relevant than other functions such as write_md_to_word, write_report_introduction, and write_report. By clicking on the write_md_to_pdf node, the analyst quickly identified as the taint sink candidate the API call md2pdf (id 30064773841) in the variable plane.

Variable-level taint source candidate identification. The analyst then inspected 8 RR nodes to identify the taint source. Upon examining the function names, the analyst identified the most relevant functions to retrieve content from knowledge base: DocumentLoader._load_document, AzureDocumentLoader.load, and LangChainDocumentLoa
der.load. By examining the variable plane of the 3 functions, the analyst determined that they are for retrieving knowledge from a local file, a cloud file, and in-memory vectors, respectively. Based on the user report that the knowledge base was stored locally, the analyst deduced that the API call loader.load (id 30064778131) in DocumentLoader._load_
document could be the taint source candidate.

Variable-level query to identify the CEP. With all of these, the analyst submitted a variable-level query: CHECK node.30064773841 DEPENDS_ON node.30064778131. The query returned 4 paths, one of which is the correct path that the malicious content took to cause the harm in the particular incident. The CEP in the motivating example was identified thereby. As shown in Figure 6(b), the malicious content from the knowledge base was combined with the crawled web page in the PK (red) before going to the LLM context window and generating the report.

C.3. Case Study 3: SWE-agent IPI

Incident. SWE-agent fetched a GitHub issue to begin a software engineering task. The issue body was embedded with invisible malicious instructions. The SWE-agent followed the instructions in the issue and caused the target software to delay showing the user interface for 10,000 seconds, which appeared to be a denial-of-service to the user.

Log investigation. The analyst triaged the trajectory log and obtained two key observations. First, the task originated from a GitHub issue. Second, the agent applied a patch that inserted a denial-of-service delay into the target repository’s source code.

Region-level query. Following the workflow in Case Study 1, the analyst submitted a region-level query CHECK (PK DEPENDS_ON PA) AND (PA DEPENDS_ON PK), which returns 47 functions (26 in PA, 2 in PK). The analyst knew that only the the 26 PA nodes needed to be examined.

Variable-level taint source candidate identification. The analyst started with the 26 PA-region nodes. Since the attack entered through a GitHub issue, the analyst searched for functions related to fetching issue content. By searching github in function names, the analyst found two relevant functions: _get_problem_statement_from_github_issue and GithubIssue.get_problem_statement. The analyst clicked to examine the variable planes of these two functions and identified the taint source as the API call api.issues.get (id 30064790320) in _get_problem_statement_from_gith
ub_issue.

Variable-level taint sink candidate identification. The analyst continued inspecting the 26 PA-region nodes to identify the taint sink. Since the attack effect was modification of source code in the target repository, the analyst looked for functions that apply code changes. By examining function names, only _apply_patch is most relevant to applying patches. The analyst clicked to examine its variable plane and identified the taint sink as the API call subprocess.run (id 30064783612) in SaveApplyPatchHook._apply_patch.

Variable-level query to identify the CEP. With the taint source and taint sink identified, the analyst submitted a variable-level query: CHECK node.30064783612 DEPENDS_ON node.30064790320. The query returns 1 path passing through 21 functions (Figure 9(b)). The path traces data from _get_pr
oblem_statement_from_github_issue (PA) through get_
problem_statement into the agent’s message history construction (_get_format_dict, _add_templated_messages_
to_history), then through the agent’s forward loop (forward
_with_handling, forward, handle_action, handle_submis
sion), and finally to the patch application hooks (on_instance
_completed, _save_patch, _apply_patch), where subproce
ss.run executes git apply.

CEP identified. The results showed that the CEP of the attack incident is the API call api.issues.get in the _get_pro
blem_statement_from_github_issue function that fetches the GitHub issue content containing the malicious instructions at line 96 in the file sweagent/utils/github.py.

C.4. Case Study 4: Quivr IPI + MC-Poison (KB)

Incident. An attacker compromised a user-trusted website. The user then used Quivr’s crawl functionality to add the website’s content to a personal knowledge base, unknowingly storing the malicious content as document embeddings. Days later, when the user asked questions about the topic covered by the compromised page, the application retrieved the malicious content and produced manipulated responses.

Log investigation. The analyst triaged the log and obtained two key observations: the user had crawled a URL into a knowledge base, and the user later received manipulated responses when asking questions against the same knowledge base.

From knowledge base retrieval to the manipulated response. The analyst first investigated how the malicious content in the knowledge base reaches the chat response. The analyst submitted CHECK (PK DEPENDS_ON RR) AND (Per DEPENDS_ON PK), which returns a graph of 21 nodes (3 in Per, 1 in PK, 5 in RR). The analyst began with the 3 Per nodes to identify the taint sink. Following the same process as in Case Study 1 (Section C.1), the analyst identified update_chat_history and the variable (id 30064774368), the API call that persists the LLM response to the chat history, as the taint sink.

The analyst then inspected the 5 RR nodes to identify the taint source. Two functions are relevant to data retrieval: get_chat_history and CustomSupabaseVectorStore.sim
ilarity_search. By examining their variable planes, the analyst found that get_chat_history retrieves multi-round conversation records, while similarity_search retrieves document chunks from the knowledge base. Since the malicious content was stored in the knowledge base, the analyst identified the API call that queries the vector store for similar documents (id 146028888356) in similarity_search as the taint source.

With these, the analyst submitted a variable-level query: CHECK node.30064774368 DEPENDS_ON node.146028888356. The query returns 1 path (Figure 8(a), phase A (left)). The path traces data from similarity_search (RR) through _construct_prompt (PK, where the retrieved documents are injected into the LLM prompt as context) to the LLM call and finally to update_chat_history (Per), confirming that the malicious content stored in the knowledge base reached the LLM context window and polluted the chat response.

From crawled website to knowledge base storage. The taint source identified above (similarity_search) reads from the knowledge base but is not the CEP. The analyst must determine how the malicious content entered the knowledge base in the first place. Since the log shows that the user added external content to the knowledge base through the crawl functionality, the analyst submitted CHECK RR DEPENDS_ON PA, which returns a graph of 47 nodes (12 in PA, 25 in RR).

The result graph contains two disconnected subgraphs (Figure 5): one centered around crawl_endpoint and the crawl-related functions (CrawlWebsite._crawl, CrawlWeb
site.process), the other centered around the chat handlers (create_question_handler, create_chat_handler). Since the analyst has already confirmed that the malicious content resides in the knowledge base rather than the chat history, the chat subgraph does not need to be examined. The analyst focused on the crawl subgraph, which contains 3 PA nodes and 16 RR nodes.

The analyst started with the 3 PA nodes to identify the taint source. These three functions, CrawlWebsite._crawl, CrawlWebsite.process, and crawl_endpoint, form a single call chain, where crawl_endpoint calls process, which in turn calls _crawl. Since the taint source must be the entry point where untrusted external content first enters the application, the analyst examined the innermost function _crawl, which sends an HTTP request to retrieve the webpage content. By examining its variable plane, the analyst identified the API call that fetches the webpage (id 30064771354) as the taint source.

The analyst then inspected the 16 RR nodes to identify the taint sink. When the analyst examined the function names, most nodes were file-processing utilities or content parsers unrelated to knowledge base storage. Only Neurons.create_
vector directly suggests the function is writing to the vector store. By examining its variable plane, the analyst identified the API call that stores document embeddings into the knowledge base (id 30064776465) as the taint sink.

The analyst submitted a variable-level query: CHECK node.
30064776465 DEPENDS_ON node.30064771354. The query returns 1 path passing through 10 functions (Figure 8(a), phase B (right)). The path traces data from _crawl (PA), through file processing and content parsing, to create_vector (RR), where the malicious content was embedded and stored in the knowledge base.

CEP identified. The analyst connected the two paths through the knowledge base: the crawl path writes the malicious content into the same knowledge base that the chat path later retrieves from. Although the write occurred days before the read, the log confirmed that both operations targeted the same knowledge base. The CEP of the incident is the API call that fetches the webpage in CrawlWebsite._crawl at line 19 of backend/crawl/crawler.py.

Appendix D CEPs + Paths identified in all incidents

We show the function-level paths identified in all eight incidents, except for the one (Quivr MC-Poison (M)) that is already included in the main body of the paper (Figure 2(b)). The CEPs are identified as the source node of the path in the five single-phase incidents; for the other two incidents (Quivr MC-Poison (KB) and Quivr IPI + MC-Poison (KB)), the CEPs are identified as the source node of the path in Phase B.

Appendix E Failure Analysis of Existing Tools

Existing static taint analyzers do not support end-to-end CEP identification. We therefore provide the ground-truth CEP as the source and the operation capturing the attack effect as the sink. We evaluate whether their outputs satisfy the tool-specific success criteria for verifying the given CEP. We then examine the causes that prevent verification of the given CEP in Table 4. The used tool versions are: Joern 4.0.360, CodeQL CLI 2.27.0 with codeql/python-all 7.2.5, and Pysa 0.9.25. Table 11 reports the findings for every incident, phase, and tool; the following subsections explain selected examples.

E.1. Unresolved Indirect Call Targets

An incomplete call graph omits possible targets of a call. When an unresolved callee returns a tainted value, the analyzer may fail to propagate that taint to the caller.

In GPT-Researcher’s IPI case, scraper.scrape_async() retrieves webpage content and returns it to the caller, which assigns it to content (Listing 5, #6). Pysa cannot resolve which function this call invokes, so it cannot propagate the tainted webpage content returned by that function to content. Pysa’s fallback taint model propagates taint from arguments to a call’s return value. However, scrape_async() takes no explicit arguments: the webpage content is retrieved inside the callee, rather than passed into the call. The fallback therefore does not mark the returned value, or content, as tainted.

Pysa also cannot resolve the target of browse_urls (Listing 5, #11), which prevents the returned tainted value from reaching scraped_content. In our diagnostic experiment, we added type casts to a copy of the application’s source code and reran Pysa. The casts tell Pysa to treat scraper as a NoDriverScraper and self.researcher.scraper_manager as a BrowserManager. With both casts, Pysa reported the call to write_md_to_pdf at main.py:28, indicating that its report argument contains tainted webpage content. This call lies on the expected attack path and therefore satisfies our Pysa success criterion. With either cast alone, Pysa did not report this call.

In Quivr’s KB exploitation, self.vector_store is a CustomSupabaseVectorStore object. The call to its similarity_search method (Listing 6, #2) retrieves KB documents and returns them at #5. Joern and CodeQL cannot identify this method as the target of the call. Both tools mark documents at #5 as a taint source, but neither propagates that taint to the value returned by the call at #2. In a copy of Quivr’s source code, we replaced the call at #2 with the call at #8–#10 and reran both tools. The replacement names the class’s method directly, passes the vector-store object explicitly, and keeps the same query. Both tools then identified the method and marked the call’s return value as tainted. However, this change alone did not recover the complete source-to-sink path; Table 11 lists the other causes.

E.2. Missing Data Dependencies Through Language Constructs

Taint propagation can be interrupted when an analyzer does not fully represent the data dependencies of a language construct (e.g., nested dictionary accesses, comprehension). This includes argument binding, container accesses, object construction, and field access.

In SWE-agent’s IPI case, tool_call["function"]["arguments"] reads the tool call’s arguments through two nested dictionary accesses (Listing 7, #2). The first retrieves the dictionary describing the requested function; the second retrieves a JSON string containing the argument names and values. json.loads converts this string into the Python dictionary values. Joern represents both accesses but omits the data-dependence edge from the first access’s result to the second access. Consequently, taint reaches the inner dictionary but not the argument string. In a source-code copy, we separated the accesses into function = tool_call["function"] and values = json.loads(function["arguments"]). With the other diagnostic changes held fixed, Joern then propagated taint to values without an additional JSON-decoding model.

In GPT-Researcher’s IPI case, CodeQL fails to propagate taint through an awaited tuple return. The tuple returned by scrape_async() contains webpage text, which the caller assigns to content (Listing 5, #5–#7). CodeQL does not carry the text’s taint across the await expression to this variable. Summaries that propagate the contained values across the affected await expressions, together with the call and API models in Table 11, allow CodeQL to report a source-to-PDF path containing the required functions.

Argument binding is separate from resolving the called function. For example, in Quivr’s memory-exploitation case, replacing the named arguments to update_chat_history with positional arguments lets Joern propagate the answer into self.assistant. An additional constructor-content rule is needed for that taint to reach the constructed object returned to the caller.

E.3. Missing Data Dependencies Across API Calls

An API call may read, transform, or store data. To follow tainted data through the call, the analyzer needs to know what the API does with it. The analyzer can obtain this information by analyzing the API’s implementation or using a summary that describes how data flows through the API. If the relevant behavior is neither analyzed nor summarized, the analyzer may lose track of the tainted data at the call. We include database insertion/readback within an API operation here; separate writes and later reads across application stages belong to Section E.4.

In Quivr’s memory-exploitation case, the application supplies stored user and assistant messages to a model chain to generate a new answer. It then stores the answer in the database, constructs a ChatHistory object from the returned record, and returns that object from the handler. After we supplied rules connecting the configured history source to its message fields, CodeQL propagated taint to the model-chain input but not its result (Listing 8, #2). We added a summary relating the request dictionary to the call result. CodeQL then tracked taint into the generated answer and the record passed to the database insertion, but not into the returned database data (#5–#10). Adding a second summary relating the inserted record to the returned data allowed taint to reach the input of ChatHistory. A separate field-read probe confirmed that taint subsequently reached the returned object’s assistant field.

E.4. Missing Data Dependencies Through Stored Data

Tracking taint through stored data requires the analysis to connect a write to a subsequent read of the same data. Without this connection, taint on the written value may not propagate to the value read from a file, database, or object field.

In the non-GitHub branch examined for Quivr’s compound-attack poisoning phase, the crawler writes webpage text to a file (Listing 9, #5). The handler opens that file and copies its contents into spooled_file (#12–#13), which it then wraps for upload. The crawler returns only names derived from the URL (#7); the webpage text reaches the handler through the file contents. In the evaluated configurations, Joern, CodeQL, and Pysa do not connect the write to this later use, so they do not propagate the webpage taint into the uploaded content.

An explicit file-transfer model connects the written webpage content to the upload object. With this model and the other dependencies in Table 11, Joern and CodeQL report paths from the crawler source to the document argument of add_documents. Pysa’s model uses an instrumented source copy that exposes the written content to a helper returning the upload object. Pysa reports filter_file in crawl_endpoint, identifying its file argument at crawl_routes.py:62 as carrying crawler taint to the configured create_vector sink. Its aggregate object model does not distinguish loaded document text from metadata.

Appendix F Details of Knowledge Collection

F.1. Structured Prompt Example

Listing 10 shows a simplified prompt used to label Quivr’s get_chat_history. The listing has four parts: the labeling task, code and supporting information, decision rules, and the required answer. The task and decision rules are supplied in a system message, while the code and supporting information are supplied in a user message. We also specify the fields that the LLM’s answer must contain and require it to return them in JSON. The listing abbreviates documents, code, and repeated metadata while retaining all six calls to be classified.

1. Labeling task. The task is to determine the function’s EXT or INT label from its direct accesses to information sources. For each call in record.api_calls, the LLM reports whether it directly accesses an external (EXT) information source, an internal (INT) information source, both types, neither, or cannot be classified from the supplied evidence. The function’s label is then computed from these findings.

An information source supplies or receives information used in the application’s tasks. EXT denotes a source through which the application obtains new task information or communicates with users, LLMs, or external services, such as user input, model responses, or public web content. INT denotes a source that the application maintains for use across tasks, such as its stored conversation history or knowledge base. A function can receive an INT label even when it accesses information over a network. For example, a function that retrieves the application’s stored conversation history from a remote database accesses an INT source.

2. Code and supporting information. The user message contains six components, each with a separate purpose.

Function and call record (record). The function_key identifies the target function by file and name; api_calls lists the operations to classify. Each call has an identifier (a0–a5), a source location, and details recording the operation called, the object it is called on, and the arguments passed to it. The tmp names denote intermediate values in the analysis representation. For example, tmp0 holds the query built by the preceding database operations, so tmp0.execute() runs that query. This call is listed as a0. Call a5 represents adding each ChatHistory(message) value to the result list. The analysis makes this list-building step explicit as tmp5.append(ChatHistory(message)), where tmp5 is the result list. Thus, a5 refers to append, which adds the value to the list; ChatHistory(message) creates the value being added.

Labeling guidance (knowledge.documents). The prompt includes four documents containing rules and examples to help the LLM judge whether a call directly accesses an EXT or INT information source. Developers can extend this guidance by adding documents or updating the rules and examples to cover additional cases. The current documents explain how to classify only the outermost call in a nested call expression, exclude in-memory operations from information-source accesses, and determine whether a file or URL provides EXT or INT task information. For example, in items.append(read_file(path)), the outermost call append only modifies an in-memory list; it does not perform the file access. Classifying read_file(path) requires additional evidence about the file: a public document is an EXT source, whereas the application’s stored conversation history is an INT source.

Code excerpts (source). Code excerpts can help the LLM understand what each listed call does and how its inputs and outputs are used. The excerpts include the target function and its calling context, such as code around the call site, argument definitions, and uses of the returned values. Each excerpt includes an identifier for citation, its file path and line numbers, and the code itself. In this example, the target function queries the chat_history table using chat_id, and its caller passes self.chat_id as the argument.

Static analysis results (supporting_evidence). The prompt also provides program-analysis results that identify possible callees and show how values reach each call’s receiver and arguments. These results help the LLM trace which information source a call accesses. Each result identifies the listed call it describes and references the corresponding code excerpt. The supporting evidence also includes whether each call was resolved to an application-defined function. For example, a0, tmp0.execute(), is marked not_resolved_to_application, indicating that no application-defined callee was identified.

Coverage summary (overview). Even when the full function is supplied, the LLM may still need evidence from elsewhere in the application to determine whether a call accesses an EXT or INT information source. The coverage summary helps the LLM assess whether the supplied evidence is sufficient to classify each call. It reports the number of calls to be classified, the source-code line ranges supplied, and any evidence that could not be retrieved or was omitted.

Response reminder (next_action). The LLM must return a finding for every listed call using the supplied evidence. It cannot request additional evidence or invoke tools.

3. Decision rules. The LLM assigns one of six call-level decisions to each listed call based on the supplied evidence:

  • •

    EXT: the call directly accesses an EXT source.

  • •

    INT: the call directly accesses an INT source.

  • •

    both: the call directly accesses both EXT and INT sources. This finding requires evidence of both accesses, rather than uncertainty between the two types.

  • •

    application_call: all identified candidate callees are application-defined functions. Their information-source accesses are assessed separately within those functions.

  • •

    no_source_access: the call does not directly access a task information source, such as a call that only formats text or modifies an in-memory list.

  • •

    unresolved: the supplied evidence is insufficient to assign a finding. The LLM must state what information is missing.

The available decisions depend on the callee information supplied for each call. A possible application-defined callee excludes EXT, INT, and both; application_call is available only when all candidate callees are application-defined. In Listing 10, none of the six calls has an identified application-defined callee, so application_call is unavailable.

Each decision applies only to the listed call. For a nested call expression, the LLM classifies the outermost call without attributing the inner calls’ information-source accesses to it. Every listed call must receive a decision, including calls in alternative branches.

4. Required answer. The LLM returns a report explaining its call-level decisions for developer review. For each listed call, the report contains one of the six decisions defined above, a brief explanation, and references to supporting code excerpts. The report also provides an overall explanation, identifies the labeling-guidance documents used, and lists any missing information needed to classify unresolved calls. Listing 11 shows the report entry for a5: the decision is no_source_access, and the explanation states that appending a constructed value to a list does not access an information source. The entry also references supporting code. The remaining report entries are omitted for brevity.

F.2. Detailed LLM Inference Results

Table 12 reports the LLM-assisted labeling results for the 2,719 candidate functions across the five applications, before developer review and correction. Note that the application functions that do not call any built-in or library APIs do not need a label (Section 6.1). They are excluded in the results.

For each candidate function, the call-level decisions are combined to propose an EXT or INT label. The function receives no label (skip) if its calls access neither source type or both types. If the supplied evidence is insufficient to determine whether the function should receive a label, the function remains unresolved.

The Decided column counts candidate functions that receive an EXT, INT, or skip decision. The Unresolved column counts candidate functions requiring additional inspection before a decision can be made. The two N columns report how many functions receive proposed EXT and INT labels, respectively; the remaining decided functions receive skip. All proposed decisions still require developer review for correctness validation.

For each label type, FNR is the fraction of candidate functions requiring that label that do not receive it, while FPR is the fraction of candidate functions not requiring that label that incorrectly receive it. Both rates consider only functions with an EXT, INT, or skip decision and a known reference label. Functions that remain unresolved are excluded. Thus, a zero FNR does not mean that all functions requiring the label have been identified; some may remain unresolved.

F.3. Developer Report-Review Examples

The following examples show how developers review the LLM reports from the evaluation in Section 10.8. They cover three cases: accepting a correct label, correcting an incorrect label, and resolving a case where the LLM could not reach a decision. Each listing shows (1) the candidate function and its calls, (2) the code needed to understand them, (3) the LLM report, and (4) the steps a developer would take to determine the function’s label. It also explains what the developer would need to inspect without the report. The reports are shortened for readability while preserving the original decisions and explanations.

Correct label: review and accept EXT. Listing 12 shows the report for GPT-Researcher’s BingSearch.search. The report proposes EXT because the function sends the agent’s search query to Bing and retrieves web results. It identifies the HTTP call that performs this access and explains why the other six calls, which format, parse, log, or collect results, do not directly access information sources. The developer can follow the cited code to verify the search request, the returned content, and the explanations for the remaining calls before accepting EXT. The proposed label matches the reference label used in the evaluation.

Incorrect label: review and remove EXT. Listing 13 shows the report for aider’s check_version. The report proposes EXT because call a3 retrieves the latest aider version from PyPI. However, the supplied code compares this version with the installed version to check for an application update; it does not retrieve information for the user’s coding task. The developer therefore changes a3’s decision to no_source_access and checks that the remaining calls also access no task information sources. The function then receives a skip decision, recorded as NA in the developer-knowledge table. The report has already identified the network request and the returned version; the developer needs to correct why that information does not qualify for an EXT label.

Unresolved label: inspect additional code to determine INT. Listing 14 shows the report for Quivr’s get_chat_history, the function used in the earlier prompt example. The report leaves the function unresolved because the supplied code does not establish how the database client is created or whether the retrieved history is reused to answer later questions. The developer checks additional code to confirm that the query uses a Supabase client and that the retrieved conversation history is passed to the LLM when answering a new question. This evidence supports an INT label. The listing shows the additional code separately from the code supplied to the LLM. The evaluation still counts the original LLM result as unresolved; the INT label is determined through developer inspection.
